entry.title: Robust Global Testing for Mean Functions in Sparse and Dense Functional and Longitudinal Data

link.title: Robust Global Testing for Mean Functions in Sparse and Dense Functional and Longitudinal Data

entry.content: We develop a robust quadratic score test for a specified mean function in functional and longitudinal data. The construction combines a convex loss with subject-level scores while retaining dependence among repeated measurements. An explicit score-centering condition ensures that the target remains the population mean. We establish the null distribution and Sobolev separation rates under sparse and dense sampling, identifying a transition from a nonparametric testing rate to the root-n boundary. A Gaussian multiplier bootstrap remains valid across these regimes, including settings with non-Gaussian quadratic limits. For implementation, we use a finite spline approximation and estimate the curvature through symmetric score increments. Under the stated conditions, the feasible procedure preserves null calibration and attains a consistency separation rate matching the lower bound over model classes containing a Gaussian submodel. Simulations illustrate the performance of squared, Huber, and absolute losses under regular errors and contamination, and an analysis of longitudinal CD4 counts demonstrates the method.

entry.title: Compartment-driven Gaussian processes for uncertainty quantification of pharmacokinetic exposures

link.title: Compartment-driven Gaussian processes for uncertainty quantification of pharmacokinetic exposures

entry.content: Pharmacokinetic modeling is a crucial part of drug development. An important goal is to estimate patients’ total and peak exposure to a drug over time, quantified by the area under the concentration–time curve (AUC) and the maximum concentration ($C_{\max}$) respectively. Such exposure assessment is essential to balance efficacy and safety in medications that offer therapeutic benefits but carry risks of toxicity, such as chemotherapy drugs. Uncertainty quantification for exposure quantities, however, remains challenging, since they are functionals of an often sparsely observed concentration–time curve with measurement errors. We propose a compartment-driven Gaussian process framework that propagates uncertainty in concentration–time curves to pharmacokinetic exposure functionals. Our approach uses pharmacokinetic compartmental models to specify a mechanistically informed prior and Gaussian processes to accommodate departures from the assumed pharmacokinetic dynamics. The framework can accommodate both individual-level and group-aggregated concentration–time data commonly seen in practice. We provide straightforward computational procedures for drawing posterior inference on AUC and $C_{\max}$. Simulations across a range of observation schemes demonstrate robustness to departures from the assumed compartmental dynamics. We apply the method to patient-level datasets on warfarin and theophylline, and aggregated data from a chemotherapy study of 5-fluorouracil and capecitabine in patients with normal or impaired hepatic function. The chemotherapy analysis quantifies drug-specific exposure differences between groups with differing liver function, with potential implications for informing dosing decisions.

entry.title: Optimal approximation error approach in Bayesian inverse problems

link.title: Optimal approximation error approach in Bayesian inverse problems

entry.content: In many inverse problems, evaluating the forward operator is computationally expensive, making it common practice to accelerate inference with a less costly approximate model. However, such approximations introduce unwanted bias and must be carefully accounted for to ensure the reliability of the solution. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced in Bayesian inference, where accurate posterior characterisation typically requires a large number of forward model evaluations. More precisely, AEM incorporates the model error into the additive Gaussian noise distribution. A central challenge in this approach is how to choose the modified noise mean and covariance in a principled way. To address this, we propose a new framework, optimal approximation error (OAE) which determines the noise model by minimising the expected information loss, measured via the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the true and approximate posterior distributions. We show that the standard enhanced error approach (EEA) is recovered as the minimiser of the expected divergence between likelihoods rather than posteriors and develop OAE as a direct alternative targeting posterior accuracy. We establish bi-convexity of the OAE objective, introduce a regularised, provably convergent proximal alternating minimisation scheme, and derive closed-form expressions in the Gaussian linear setting. We further show that OAE estimates computed from empirical training data are statistically consistent. Numerical experiments on a linear CT problem and a nonlinear Darcy-flow problem show that OAE improves posterior accuracy relative to both the uncorrected and EEA-corrected likelihoods.

entry.title: Distributional Flexibility under Box-Cox Normality: A Theoretical and Empirical Evaluation of the Power-Normal Distribution

link.title: Distributional Flexibility under Box-Cox Normality: A Theoretical and Empirical Evaluation of the Power-Normal Distribution

entry.content: Methods based on Box-Cox models have recently been developed for inference on clinically interpretable treatment effects in clinical trials. These methods model marginal outcome distributions using the power-normal distribution (PND), but the range of real-world data distributions that it can adequately approximate remains unclear. We evaluated PND approximations using two parameterizations of the four-parameter generalized $F$/generalized beta of the second kind family and 165 laboratory variables from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. Overall distributional agreement was assessed using the overlap coefficient and Jensen-Shannon divergence, and location and spread on the original scale were evaluated using relative biases in the median and interquartile range. The PND closely approximated a broad range of smooth unimodal positive distributions in both the theoretical and empirical evaluations. Reduced agreement was associated with pronounced lower-bound accumulation, heaping or discretization, and multicomponent or peak-tail features. These features may be recognizable before fitting and provide practical guidance for assessing the suitability of the PND. We also developed the R package powerNormal for distributional calculations, parameter estimation, reparameterization, and random-number generation for the PND.

entry.title: Assessing the Role of Green Premium and Localized Price Spillovers in Budget Hotels : Evidence from Delhi National Capital Region (NCR)

link.title: Assessing the Role of Green Premium and Localized Price Spillovers in Budget Hotels : Evidence from Delhi National Capital Region (NCR)

entry.content: Sustainable urban tourism depends on how environmental quality, public transport accessibility, and accommo dation clustering shape visitor mobility and destination development. This study examines these relationships in the budget hotel sector of Delhi National Capital Region, India, an emerging mega-destination marked by rapid urban expansion and uneven infrastructure provision. Using data from 857 budget hotels, we estimate a mixed geographically weighted spatial autoregressive model that captures both spatial heterogeneity and localized price spillovers. The model combines hotel attributes with satellite- derived indicators, including vegetation density, built-up area, night-time light intensity, and distances to metro stations, bus stops, airports, city centers, and tourist attractions. Results show that greenery has a place-dependent value: it generates a green premium in dense urban cores, where environmental amenities are scarce, but becomes a discount in peripheral areas where vegetation often reflects weaker tourism infrastructure. Metro accessibility creates a mobility pre mium, highlighting the role of public transport in supporting low-cost tourist movement. Local spatial spillovers reveal agglomeration benefits in established clusters and price cannibalization in peripheral markets. The find ings show how spatially differentiated planning can align green infrastructure, transit investment, and budget accommodation with more sustainable urban tourism development.

entry.title: Integrating multi-source local information for global undirected graph reconstruction via integer programming

link.title: Integrating multi-source local information for global undirected graph reconstruction via integer programming

entry.content: Graphical models are widely used to represent conditional independence structures, but learning them is challenging when data are fragmented across sources that measure different subsets of variables and may not be directly shareable. We develop a general framework for reconstructing a shared global graph from heterogeneous, partially observed sources. Our framework permits both the observed variable sets and source-specific distributions to differ. Under a source-wise faithfulness condition, local conditional independence graphs correspond to latent projections of the shared global graph, which is identifiable up to the equivalence class induced by the observed variable sets. The framework integrates raw data, estimated source graphs, or a combination of both, accommodating settings with restricted access to individual-level data, such as privacy constraints. We develop mixed-integer optimization formulations and scalable approximate algorithms for several classes of graphical models. Unlike standard high-dimensional analyses, our guarantees are governed by new combinatorial notions of signal strength that capture how information propagates across partially observed sources. Extensive simulations further show that integration can substantially improve estimation of source-specific projected graphs relative to separate source methods. Real-data application illustrates the framework’s use with partially-observed sources of fatty acid measurements.

entry.title: Metropolized backward sampling for conditional sequential Monte Carlo

link.title: Metropolized backward sampling for conditional sequential Monte Carlo

entry.content: Particle Gibbs samplers with backward sampling are widely used for sampling the smoothing distribution of state-space models, but, with few particles, the new trajectory often coincides with the current one at many time steps. A known but rarely used remedy replaces the random selection of the final particle by a Metropolis–Hastings move which avoids the current particle. We show that, with backward sampling, this remedy only helps at the last time steps, because its effect on the update rates decays geometrically with the distance to the final time. We propose instead Metropolized backward sampling, which makes such a move at every step of the backward pass, forcibly switching trajectories whenever possible. Additionally, we introduce a coupled version which prevents proposing the current trajectory, maximizing the chances of an actual switch versus the current trajectory and performing perfect sampling when the state-space model has no observations, a feature not shared by backward sampling. We prove that, at every time step, both methods dominate backward sampling as they update the state more often and have smaller lag-one autocorrelations than it does. Our methods are drop-in replacements for backward sampling, and can be used to improve any particle Gibbs sampler.

entry.title: Pinpointing Pivot Points: The DECIDE Framework for Data Analysis Decision Importances

link.title: Pinpointing Pivot Points: The DECIDE Framework for Data Analysis Decision Importances

entry.content: Human judgment calls made throughout the data science life cycle can change the conclusions drawn from data. Independent analysts often make different choices when given the same data, leading to often unacceptable variations in results and contributing to the ongoing reproducibility crisis across scientific disciplines. The rapid adoption of agentic tools threatens to amplify this crisis. Several approaches have been developed to address this variation by following the same strategy: repeating an analysis under different combinations of analytical decisions and inspecting the distribution of outcomes. Examples include multiverse analysis, specification curve analysis, and vibration of effects. More broadly, the Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) framework assesses how documented judgment calls across the data science life cycle affect conclusions, with predictability serving as a reality-check that a model captures signal. Each of these approaches results in a “multiverse” object. While the distribution of outcomes reflects the overall variability of conclusions, estimating the influence of each individual decision requires additional tools. A common heuristic is to train a model to predict the outcome from these decisions and treat its coefficients or feature importances as proxies for each decision’s influence. Although this strategy may work in certain cases, it assumes the model is correctly specified and accurately predicts the outcome, which we show is not always the case. In this work, we introduce DECIDE, a model-free framework that quantifies each decision’s importance from the actual outcomes across the plausible decision space, avoiding issues of predictability by design. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DECIDE by applying it to real-world multiverse analyses. We further provide what is, to our knowledge, the first formal definition of the multiverse.

entry.title: Principal-agent hypothesis testing under adaptive experimentation

link.title: Principal-agent hypothesis testing under adaptive experimentation

entry.content: Principal-agent hypothesis testing studies statistical contracts in which a principal rewards an agent according to data the agent generates. Existing work focuses on the single-shot setting, where the agent produces a single dataset. We extend the framework to sequential settings, where evidence accumulates over time, rewards may be deferred to the end or disbursed incrementally, and the agent may stop the contract at a strategically chosen stopping time. We call a contract null-deterring if no ‘‘null agent’’ (those whose data-generating distribution lies in the null hypothesis) can profit in expectation under any stopping rule, and our main conceptual result shows that such contracts are characterized by e-processes. We then turn to the agent’s best response and identify the optimal stopping rule through the Snell envelope of the reward process. We develop simpler, more interpretable approximations that often require the agent to have only partial knowledge of its distribution.

entry.title: Proximal R2 Priors for Structured Variance Allocation

link.title: Proximal R2 Priors for Structured Variance Allocation

entry.content: Scientific domain knowledge in regression often concerns structural relationships among model terms, which are typically encoded as parameter constraints. Since such relationships rarely hold exactly in practice, prior distributions should encourage them while at the same time retaining support for scientifically plausible departures. Accounting for these relationships becomes more pressing in modern regression, where high-dimensionality is usually present and regularisation is essential. $R^2$ decomposition priors provide an interpretable foundation for regularisation by placing a prior on total explained variance and distributing the implied signal across model terms. We introduce the Proximal R2 prior, which uses proximal relaxations to encode these relationships as soft constraints on the variance allocation. Our formulation yields differentiable posteriors compatible with standard gradient based samplers. Theoretically, we prove that our prior preserves the characteristic marginal properties of global-local shrinkage priors. Moreover, we establish posterior consistency and contraction rates in growing dimensions, showing that the inclusion of structural relationships and proximal methods do not alter the shrinkage properties. Notably, these results demonstrate that the structural constraints in the model do not hinder posterior recovery. Simulation studies and real-data applications to interaction and generalised additive models demonstrate that our prior improves parameter recovery, out-of-sample prediction, and sampling efficiency over existing constrained and unconstrained shrinkage priors, even under structural misspecification.

entry.title: The Hidden Value of Soft Infrastructure for Urban Flood Adaptation

link.title: The Hidden Value of Soft Infrastructure for Urban Flood Adaptation

entry.content: As sea level rises and flooding events become more frequent, cities are tapping into a range of engineering and planning solutions to reduce flood losses. Beyond traditional hard'' infrastructure (e.g., sewage, seawalls),soft’’ infrastructure that supports and empowers the role of citizens in preparedness has been hailed as a promising avenue for improving adaptation. Despite its promise, there have been very limited attempts to quantify its effectiveness in reducing losses relative to hard infrastructure, particularly in urban environments. This study fills this knowledge gap using generative AI to quantify the effectiveness of a range of hard and soft infrastructure in urban areas. We demonstrate, for the first time, that soft infrastructure can significantly reduce flood losses, with an impact on par with hard infrastructure. Our results open the door to novel ways of confronting adaptation challenges in cities. Soft infrastructure is a viable alternative, especially when budgetary or time constraints make hard infrastructure unattainable. Policymakers should also couple soft and hard infrastructure to maximize resilience.

entry.title: An Analysis of High-Dimensional Land-Water Transitions in the Great Lakes via a Bayesian Discrepancy Model for Multinomial Data

link.title: An Analysis of High-Dimensional Land-Water Transitions in the Great Lakes via a Bayesian Discrepancy Model for Multinomial Data

entry.content: Global water-level systems have undergone large changes in recent years. Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) land cover data can be used to monitor and understand these changes. However, such data are extremely high-dimensional making them difficult to process while accounting for all sources of uncertainty. Bayesian hierarchical models are commonly implemented using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods which can be computationally expensive for large datasets. Exact Posterior Regression (EPR) provides an efficient alternative for inference in latent Gaussian hierarchical models under exponential families without requiring MCMC or approximate Bayesian strategies. EPR has not been developed for multinomial data, and we extend this class of models to the multinomial setting. Additionally, we explore signal-to-noise covariance properties of discrepancy models, which we expect to be present in our data. We extend EPR to multinomial likelihoods via a stick-breaking construction to analyze water-level changes. Through simulation studies, we compare the proposed multinomial EPR approach with alternative models implemented using Gibbs sampling and the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA). We evaluate each approach based on regression parameter estimation, category probability estimation, and computational efficiency. Overall, EPR and INLA achieve substantial reductions in computation time while EPR shows improved metrics in estimation and prediction.

entry.title: Convex Mixed-Integer Programming for Invariant Predictions from Multi-environment Data

link.title: Convex Mixed-Integer Programming for Invariant Predictions from Multi-environment Data

entry.content: Heterogeneous data provide an opportunity to identify causal predictors by revealing which predictive relationships remain invariant. Under a linear model, we introduce a least-squares coefficient-and-risk (LSCR) invariance principle, requiring both ordinary least squares coefficients and prediction risks to remain constant across environments. Our model neither specifies an intervention mechanism nor assumes a structural causal model for the entire system. We develop an invariance score that quantifies departures from LSCR invariance and use its optimization to construct two complementary procedures for causal predictor identification. First, we propose an estimator that jointly minimizes prediction risk and invariance penalty, and establish non-asymptotic guarantees for estimation and recovery of the causal parents under suitable identifiability conditions. Second, without requiring full identifiability, we develop a testing procedure that minimizes the invariance score over all predictor sets excluding a given variable, enabling valid causal discoveries with asymptotic error control via a multiplier bootstrap. Both procedures admit convex mixed-integer optimization formulations that avoid exhaustive subset enumeration while providing certificates of optimality. Simulations and real data experiments demonstrate substantial statistical and computational improvements over existing methods.

entry.title: Noise Calibration and Exact Recovery for Multiview Ordinal Rearrangement Data

link.title: Noise Calibration and Exact Recovery for Multiview Ordinal Rearrangement Data

entry.content: We studied simultaneous recovery of a latent group count, subject partition, and signature means from multiview ordinal ranks. A normalized reference rearrangement score is an affine Spearman correlation; the problem concerns the information retained by several such scores and their noise geometry. We develop an ordered-gap estimator with direction-specific concentration radii. Its finite-sample guarantee separates signature noise, missing groups, and candidate coverage, and allows the group count to grow under an attainable-margin condition. A coordinatewise partition followed by label-tuple refinement recovers groups even when every individual coordinate has population collisions. A binary-code construction explains why the one-dimensional inverse-group margin restriction need not govern a retained coordinate bank. We derive actual-law concentration from bounded ranking modules and a fixed-dimensional combinatorial central limit theorem under an observed permutation representation. A binary ordinal submodel gives logarithmic exact-recovery information scales. A subject-effect construction distinguishes persistent overlap from reducible measurement noise, and an additional ordinal anchor quantifies how new information lowers that error floor. Five focused simulation scenarios illustrate direction-specific calibration, growing-group recovery, coordinate collision resolution, variance reduction, and the effect of an additional ordinal anchor.

entry.title: Modular Bayesian Foundation Models: Bayesian time series encoders for OOD detection, routing and forecasting

link.title: Modular Bayesian Foundation Models: Bayesian time series encoders for OOD detection, routing and forecasting

entry.content: Industrial systems continuously generate time series that vary in sampling frequency, scale, dynamics, and operating regime. Consequently a single time-series foundation model may not be able to represent all regimes effectively and retraining a large model for every new dataset or regime shift is computationally expensive. Modular foundation models address this issue by reusing specialised encoders trained on diverse datasets and by allowing the expansion of capabilities through the addition of new experts. This approach requires compact experts to minimize storage cost and a proper selection mechanism of experts for unseen data. We propose a modular foundation model framework that combines end-to-end Bayesian encoder training with uncertainty based routing. Using Singular Bayesian Neural Networks (SBNNs), we build a collection of compact Bayesian encoders whose epistemic uncertainty guides label-free selection. At the selected ranks, our Bayesian collection uses 63.8\% less storage than its deterministic counterpart. We evaluate this framework on time-series data through distribution shift, encoder selection, and probabilistic forecasting. Across seven incoming datasets, uncertainty-based routing is competitive with distance-based routing in terms of forecast MSE, while reducing average ECE from 0.086 to 0.072 and average NLL from 0.907 to 0.836. It also increases PICP90 from 82.28\% to 89.03\%. In a separate model-family comparison, we evaluate the SBNN pipeline against full-rank Bayes by Backprop, deep ensembles, and MC Dropout. The SBNN pipeline achieves an average MSE of 0.390, comparable with 0.396 for deep ensembles, 0.389 for MC dropout, and 0.443 for the full-rank Bayesian model. It uses 63.9\% fewer parameters than MC dropout, 81.9\% fewer than the full-rank model, and 92.8\% fewer than the deep ensemble.

entry.title: Tabular foundation models are not a shortcut to calibrated clinical risk prediction: a pre-registered simulation against the true risk

link.title: Tabular foundation models are not a shortcut to calibrated clinical risk prediction: a pre-registered simulation against the true risk

entry.content: Tabular foundation models are pretrained networks that predict risk from a table without fitting a model. Whether their risks are correct (calibrated) has been judged on real data, where true risk is unknown. In a pre-registered simulation with known true risks, we compared TabPFN-3.5, TabICLv2 and Mitra-v2 with Firth logistic regression with intercept correction (FLIC) in 58 scenarios and 1,000 random designs, then on four clinical data sets. Foundation models were not a shortcut to calibration. Their calibration slope matched FLIC’s within the pre-registered margin in 36 or 37 of 48 core scenarios and was better only at n = 200 with a 3% event rate. Even 3,000 patients were often not enough: with FLIC, TabPFN-3.5 or Mitra-v2, 63%-83% of samples gave risks close to the truth in average, intercept and slope at event rates of 10% and 30%, and 35%-50% at 3%. TabICLv2 did worse (8%-39% and 1%-3%). Across the random designs, foundation models had a lower true calibration error than FLIC beyond the margin in 25%-38% and a higher one in none, though small losses were predicted at n = 3000. On real data, no model resisted a change in event rate between populations; recalibration on 500 local patients largely repaired it.

entry.title: When the Same Prompt Gives Different Answers (and the Same Answer Isn’t Always Right): A Taxonomy of Failure Mechanisms, Testing, and Mitigation Strategies for LLM-Assisted Evidence Synthesis Read-and-Evaluate Tasks

link.title: When the Same Prompt Gives Different Answers (and the Same Answer Isn’t Always Right): A Taxonomy of Failure Mechanisms, Testing, and Mitigation Strategies for LLM-Assisted Evidence Synthesis Read-and-Evaluate Tasks

entry.content: LLM read-and-evaluate tasks include study screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, and critical appraisal in the evidence synthesis field. These task differ in the amount of LLM interpretation they require. Some tasks involve retrieving relatively simple information, such as an author name, sample size, or publication year. Others require the LLM to read source material, interpret it against predefined criteria, and make a judgement. Researchers should assess whether LLM judgements are accurate, supported by appropriate source evidence, and reproducible under specified conditions. A correct judgement does not necessarily indicate that the underlying evaluation process is reliable. We developed a taxonomy for identifying mechanisms that may compromise these properties and for informing the selection and reporting of appropriate evaluation methods. The taxonomy outlines potential ways that LLM judgments from read-and-evaluate tasks can fail, called TRAILS (Taxonomy of Reliability And Instability in LLM-assisted evidence Synthesis). The TRAILS taxonomy addresses two complementary questions. First, what mechanisms can cause the same read-and-evaluate task to produce different judgements across repeated LLM runs? Second, what mechanisms can systematically affect the judgement or required output in a way that is not apparent from the judgement itself? This study presents 38 mechanisms and identifies the deployment settings in which each can operate, approaches for testing them, and mitigation strategies. We also show why repeatability or accuracy does not rule out a hidden judgement failure and why human evaluation should assess whether a judgement is grounded in the supplied evidence, independent of inappropriate external influence, and produced through a process that can be examined and verified.

entry.title: Adaptive stopping and forecasting of screening, rescreening and randomization in multicentre clinical trials

link.title: Adaptive stopping and forecasting of screening, rescreening and randomization in multicentre clinical trials

entry.content: In randomised clinical trials, patients typically undergo some screening stages before randomisation. These stages complicate design as patients may be randomised after admissions to screening have been halted. Stopping the admission of new patients too late may lead to over-enrolment, as more patients than planned are randomised, increasing costs, unnecessary patient exposure and the time required to complete recruitment. Stopping too early may result in failure to achieve the planned sample size. Predictions of the stopping time should therefore account for patients currently in screening and the number of the patients to be randomised. We present a novel statistical framework for joint modelling screening and randomisation and determining an adaptive stopping time to stop admitting new patients to screening before the planned randomisation target is reached. The aim is to reduce over-enrolment while maintaining a high probability of achieving the target. We represent the screening and randomisation pathway as a multistage process with stage-specific durations and transition probabilities estimated from trial data. The model yields the distribution of the number of patients who will be randomised from the current screening pipeline and the probability of reaching the planned randomisation target. If this probability exceeds a specified threshold, such as 95% or 99%, admission of new patients to screening should be stopped. Otherwise, the model is updated as additional data accrue and is used to forecast future pipeline and the stopping time. The framework can incorporate scheduled site initiations and future closures using evolving stochastic processes, and supporting forecasts at global, regional and country levels. Illustrative simulations show that the approach can reduce over-enrolment substantially while preserving a high probability of reaching the target sample size.

entry.title: Comparing wins above replacement across baseball history

link.title: Comparing wins above replacement across baseball history

entry.content: This paper introduces iWAR, a system for estimating wins above replacement from historical Retrosheet play-by-play records. We compare its runs-allowed (RA) and fielding-independent pitching (FIP) versions with Baseball-Reference WAR (bWAR), FanGraphs WAR (fWAR) and run-based alternatives. The common historical sample contains 1,471 team-seasons across 79 years and 1,441 consecutive franchise pairs. Under the fixed conversion to wins, same-season mean absolute error was 3.695 credited wins per 162 games for iWAR RA, compared with 4.724 for bWAR and 4.744 for fWAR: reductions of 21.793% and 22.112%. The paired differences were -1.030 and -1.049, with conditional 95% calendar-block intervals of [-1.367, -0.706] and [-1.398, -0.725]. Calibration preserved most of these advantages. A broader bWAR comparison across 118 years retained a smaller advantage; modern differences were smaller or sometimes reversed. PythagenPat reconstructed records more closely than every WAR total. Next-season replay gave nearly identical fixed-map errors for iWAR FIP and fWAR, while calibration changed their ordering. An amended chronological learned-model analysis of 1,552 franchise pairs gave neural RMSE 10.163, versus 9.946 for the development-selected ridge comparator (difference +0.217; conditional interval [0.015, 0.474]). This work provides a new, specialized framework for analyzing WAR across eras and provides context for future work using learning models.

entry.title: Joint optimisation of interim timing and stopping boundaries in group sequential trials

link.title: Joint optimisation of interim timing and stopping boundaries in group sequential trials

entry.content: Group sequential designs (GSDs) are common in confirmatory trials, and their efficiency depends jointly on the timing of interim analyses and the shape of stopping boundaries. Most existing approaches optimise one component while holding the other fixed. Joint optimisation over free critical values has been studied for two- and three-stage efficacy-only designs and for tests with binding futility boundaries. Here we jointly optimise the full interim schedule and the boundary shape within the Hwang-Shih-DeCani and Kim-DeMets spending families, minimising the expected sample size under a specified alternative while controlling overall type I and type II error rates. A convex error-spending constraint prevents excessive early type I error spending. On the canonical information scale, the joint optimum depends only on the error rates, number of analyses and spending family, and is invariant to endpoint type and effect size. Without the convexity constraint, the parametric optima reproduced the unrestricted optima of Brittain & Bailey (1993) to within 0.001 in expected inflation factor. For three or more looks the jointly optimal design Pareto-dominated the scheduling-only optimal Pocock design, achieving the same or smaller expected sample size with uniformly smaller maximum sample size. Under a prespecified 1% tolerance, six analyses, five interim plus a final, captured essentially all efficiency attainable with up to seven analyses, reducing expected sample size by 23% and 33% at 80% and 90% power relative to the fixed-sample design. We illustrate the approach by redesigning the CORRECT trial.

entry.title: Zero-Complement Extrapolation: Parameter Recovery and Classification in Severely Imbalanced Logistic Regression under Rank-Deficient Regimes

link.title: Zero-Complement Extrapolation: Parameter Recovery and Classification in Severely Imbalanced Logistic Regression under Rank-Deficient Regimes

entry.content: Parameter estimation and classification in binary logistic regression deteriorate severely when the number of minority class observations ($n_1$) is smaller than the feature dimension ($p$). Under such rank-deficient rarity ($n_1 < p$), maximum likelihood estimators suffer from quasi-complete separation, penalized likelihood methods exhibit severe intercept bias, and convex minority oversampling techniques such as SMOTE collapse into an $(n_1 - 1)$-dimensional affine subspace. In this paper, we propose a novel \textit{Self-Calibrated Zero-Complement} estimator that shifts the paradigm from minority interpolation to majority fringe extrapolation. Grounded in Stein’s Lemma, we prove that the conditional expectation shift of the abundant majority class ($Y=0$) induced by logistic truncation uniquely identifies the true hyperplane normal $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ after Mahalanobis whitening. We further establish that extrapolating synthetic minority instances outward from the high-quantile density fringe of the majority distribution along the conjugate direction preserves full-rank covariance regularity ($\mathrm{rank} = p$). To accommodate both semi-supervised environments (with an unlabeled background mean) and strictly supervised subsamples, we introduce a hybrid estimator incorporating the intrinsic third-moment skewness of the majority class alongside a location-shift-invariant zero-boundary intercept calibration. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations and real-world benchmark applications (Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer and Banknote Authentication) under extreme rarity ($n_1 \in {3, 5}$) demonstrate that our approach prevents parameter divergence, recovers the oracle hyperplane with high fidelity, and substantially outperforms Firth’s regression and SMOTE in F1-score and estimation stability.

entry.title: Sparse Directed Network Recovery From Multivariate Count Time Series

link.title: Sparse Directed Network Recovery From Multivariate Count Time Series

entry.content: Count time series arise naturally in many scientific applications. Examples include species abundances collected over time, and gene expression counts over pseudotime. Network inference from such data can yield important insight into underlying biological mechanisms, but is challenging because count observations are discrete, overdispersed, and temporally dependent. We propose a multivariate Poisson log-normal model in which observed counts arise from a Poisson distribution with rates determined by a latent vector autoregressive (VAR) process. The latent VAR transition matrix induces directed temporal dependencies among components and serves as the target network parameter. We establish identifiability of the model under suitable conditions and develop two procedures for sparse estimation of the VAR transition matrix. Our first estimator is a sparse method-of-moments estimator, for which we establish consistent network recovery and parameter estimation in high-dimensional settings. Our second estimator is an L1-penalized variational inference estimator that is motivated by recent approaches for count data. We evaluate the proposed estimators through simulations under a range of sampling regimes. We further demonstrate the method on a macroinvertebrate abundance time series collected from European freshwater ecosystems, obtaining an interpretable ecological network.

link.title: Bregman projections and partition design for accelerating finite Markov chains

entry.content: We study Gibbs averaging of finite Markov chains with a prescribed stationary distribution $\pi$. Given a transition matrix $P$ and the Gibbs kernel $G$ induced by a state-space partition, we prove that $GPG$ is an information projection for every admissible Bregman generator $\phi$, with divergences defined using transition probabilities relative to $\pi$. A Pythagorean identity characterizes this projection and recovers the relative entropy and weighted Frobenius cases. A dual characterization identifies $GPG$ as a kernel closest to stationarity among those with the same projection chain as $P$; for relative entropy, it maximizes the entropy rate. The identities also give monotonicity under partition coarsening. For every reversible ergodic baseline $P$, Gibbs averaging cannot increase the squared weighted Frobenius distance to stationarity at any positive integer time, and the inequality is strict unless $P=GPG$. The corresponding mixing time therefore cannot increase. To choose the partition, we identify the divergence of $G$ from stationarity as the exact worst-case divergence of $GPG$ over all $\pi$-stationary baselines $P$. This objective depends only on the block masses. We give an exact algorithm for concave block costs, including those arising from relative entropy and power generators $\phi(u)=u^p$ with $1 2$. For power generators $\phi(u)=u^p$ with $p>1$, the objective is proportional to Tsallis entropy of order $2-p$: its minimization favors imbalanced block masses when $1 2$, while all $k$-block partitions have the same objective value when $p=2$. A numerical experiment compares the resulting projected chains with a local Metropolis sampler on a multi-modal $\pi$.

entry.title: TwinPoSI: Statistical Twins for Powerful Post-Selection Inference on Population-Based Regression Coefficients

link.title: TwinPoSI: Statistical Twins for Powerful Post-Selection Inference on Population-Based Regression Coefficients

entry.content: Post-selection inference (PoSI) quantifies uncertainty about regression coefficients after data-driven feature selection. A central question is the inferential target. Projection-based targets are the coefficients of the best linear approximation restricted to the selected features and depend on the selection procedure, whereas population-based targets are the selected features’ coefficients in the full linear model and are often more relevant for scientific interpretation. The two targets can differ, even in sign. Existing PoSI methods largely focus on projection-based targets and may yield overly wide confidence intervals. We propose TwinPoSI (statistical twin post-selection inference), a method for powerful PoSI on population-based targets with false coverage rate (FCR) control. TwinPoSI leverages \textit{statistical twins}, defined as synthetic datasets generated from a fitted model to mimic the original data. With generating parameters known, statistical twins enable direct calibration of confidence intervals for bias introduced by data-dependent feature selection. We establish that TwinPoSI controls the FCR at the nominal level, up to Monte Carlo error and an asymptotically negligible approximation error. Moreover, in a Gaussian linear model with an orthogonal design, TwinPoSI uniquely attains the oracle average interval length to first order among the methods considered. Simulations show that TwinPoSI maintains reliable FCR control for both population-based and projection-based targets while yielding shorter confidence intervals and higher power than the competing methods. In riboflavin production data, TwinPoSI identifies associated genes, quantifies their directions and magnitudes of association, and yields the shortest average intervals among the methods considered.

entry.title: Independence tests of general spatial point processes based on characteristic functions

link.title: Independence tests of general spatial point processes based on characteristic functions

entry.content: Existing nonparametric tests of spatial point process independence typically rely on random shifts to simulate their null distributions. This limits their scope to stationary point processes in rectangular study regions. Attempts to adapt random shift methods to nonrectangular study regions have resulted in significant power loss. We introduce a new type of nonparametric independence tests by taking differences of several characteristic-function-based goodness-of-fit statistics. We develop two null distribution methods for the tests without using random shifts, by making normal or symmetry assumptions on the Mercer’s expansion of the test statistics. The methods are applicable to general nonstationary point processes in study regions of any shape. In simulations, our tests based on the symmetric null distribution method have better type I error control and higher power than toroidal cross-$K$ tests in most scenarios where toroidal shifts can be applied. When tested on more general settings given appropriately-fitted marginal distributions, they still have good power and almost always control the type I error well.

entry.title: Weighted Score Matching on Bounded Domains: Nonparametric Density Estimation and Interaction Graph Recovery

link.title: Weighted Score Matching on Bounded Domains: Nonparametric Density Estimation and Interaction Graph Recovery

entry.content: We study nonparametric density estimation and interaction-graph recovery on bounded product domains using boundary-weighted score matching. In a canonically centered pairwise log-density model, graph edges are determined by bivariate interactions, but penalizing the univariate main effects can induce false edges. We derive the resulting shift in interaction scores and study partially penalized weighted score matching (P-WSM), which leaves main effects unpenalized. At the population level, P-WSM excludes edges between independent subsystems even when the marginal log densities are not represented exactly by the sieve. A nonparametric construction separates partial and joint penalization: throughout a common deterministic tuning interval, P-WSM recovers the graph while joint penalization selects a false edge. We also give growing-dimensional recovery conditions that do not require full-Gram invertibility. For density estimation at fixed dimension, we establish weighted Fisher-divergence rates and, under stronger basis-specific conditions, Kullback-Leibler and Hellinger rates for the normalized estimator. Simulations examine the benefits and limitations of partial penalization. An analysis of bone-marrow signaling data illustrates nonlinear conditional-association estimation.

entry.title: Optimal fiber comparisons for random tensors

link.title: Optimal fiber comparisons for random tensors

entry.content: We extend Seginer’s matrix norm comparison to tensors with optimal dependence on the tensor order. For a real tensor $T$ of order $k\ge2$ with centered, integrable, independent and identically distributed entries, we prove $\mathbb{E} f(T)\le\mathbb{E}\lVert T\rVert_{\mathrm{inj}} \le C\sqrt{k\log k}\,\mathbb{E} f(T)$, where $f(T)$ is the largest Euclidean norm of a one-dimensional fiber and $C$ is universal. The comparison holds for every finite rectangular format, and the entry law may depend on both the dimensions and the tensor order. We show that the factor $\sqrt{k\log k}$ is optimal by considering Rademacher tensors on $[2]^k$.

entry.title: Self-normalised change point tests that remain pivotal under non-stationarity

link.title: Self-normalised change point tests that remain pivotal under non-stationarity

entry.content: Self-normalising test statistics for time series circumvent the lag-specification of long-run variance estimators by employing an inconsistent estimator for studentization. This leads to asymptotically pivotal test distributions under stationarity, but not for nonstationary sequences. Focusing on the multiple changepoint problem, we propose an alternative self-normalised test statistic which is asymptotically pivotal even if the noise is nonstationary. Central to our argument are statistical functionals which are invariant under temporal reparametriation, i.e. clock-changes. Simulations show that the proposed procedure is more conservative than competing bootstrap procedures, but considerably more powerful against multiple changes and more reliable in terms of size for highly nonstationary time series in larger samples.

entry.title: Nonlinear Sufficient Dimension Reduction for Causal Inference with Continuous Treatments

link.title: Nonlinear Sufficient Dimension Reduction for Causal Inference with Continuous Treatments

entry.content: Causal inference with continuous treatments requires estimating nuisance functions to adjust for the potentially high-dimensional confounder, but nonparametric estimation of these functions is severely hampered by the curse of dimensionality. To address this challenge, we propose a nonlinear sufficient dimension reduction framework to construct low-dimensional sufficient confounders to preserve the unbiasedness of the treatment effect. We estimate the causal effect by combining the generalized Sliced Inverse Regression with the inverse probability weighting, outcome regression, and augmented inverse probability weighting, respectively. We further establish the convergence rates of the first two estimators and derive the asymptotic distributions of the third. Our theoretical results show that, compared to estimators based on the full covariates, dimension reduction yields faster convergence rates and weaker rate conditions without inflating the asymptotic variance. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed estimators improve finite-sample performance over their counterparts without dimension reduction, particularly when the original covariate dimension is high. These results demonstrate that sufficient dimension reduction provides a flexible approach to mitigating the curse of dimensionality in causal inference with continuous treatments.

entry.title: Challenge or Pass? A Dynamic Policy for MLB’s Automated Ball-Strike System

link.title: Challenge or Pass? A Dynamic Policy for MLB’s Automated Ball-Strike System

entry.content: Under Major League Baseball’s automated ball-strike (ABS) challenge system, players must weigh the value of overturning a call against the risk of losing a challenge they may need later. We develop a policy that values an overturn through its effect on expected runs, accounting for the count, outs, and runners on base. Using pitch tracking and game records, we reconstruct challenge opportunities, including calls that players let stand. A Bayesian model represents players’ imperfect impressions of pitch location and uses them to estimate overturn probabilities, with uncertainty calibrated from historical challenge decisions. Dynamic programming compares the expected gain with the future cost of losing a challenge, accounting for the stage of the game, the number of challenges remaining, and opportunities on both offense and defense. We develop the policy using games before the 2026 All-Star break and evaluate it without refitting on 983 games played afterward. Along the recorded sequence of opportunities, the policy recovers 0.536 modeled correction runs per game across both teams, compared with 0.452 under observed decisions, an improvement of 18.5%. The gain is 0.084 runs per game, with a 95% bootstrap interval of [0.065, 0.103]. The policy makes more challenges and recovers more value per successful review despite a lower overturn rate. These results show why overturn rate alone can be a misleading measure of challenge strategy.

entry.title: Scaling of Interface Variability in Aerospace Composite Structures: A Multi-scale Stochastic Approach from Local Identification to Panel Response

link.title: Scaling of Interface Variability in Aerospace Composite Structures: A Multi-scale Stochastic Approach from Local Identification to Panel Response

entry.content: Quantifying random spatial variations in composite interface properties is an essential prerequisite for the high-fidelity propagation of material properties variabilities through structural numerical models. This study proposes a multi-scale stochastic framework designed to bridge the gap between local interfacial characterization at the coupon scale and the global response of industrial aerospace panels, focusing specifically on the skin-stringer bond line. Building upon previous stochastic modeling and identification methodologies for Mode I fracture, we first extend the likelihood-free Bayesian calibration to Mode II configurations to characterize interfacial stochastic parameters using experimental coupon data. To address the scale-up challenge, we employ a simulation-based Stochastic Finite Element Method (SFEM) to contrast two distinct probabilistic strategies – spatially uniform variations (Paradigm 2) and spatially correlated random fields (Paradigm 3) – against the traditional industrial B-basis standard (Paradigm 1). The numerical results reveal a dual mechanism in uncertainty propagation depending on the targeted airframe design criterion. For global performance, such as the ultimate load capacity, a significant scale effect leads to an uncertainty attenuation phenomenon; statistical averaging smooths out local heterogeneities, demonstrating that a computationally efficient spatially uniform approach is sufficient. Conversely, for local integrity, such as the threshold and spatial localization of early damage initiation, the inclusion of spatially correlated random fields becomes indispensable to capture premature degradation driven by local material weak spots. This balanced probabilistic treatment offers a route toward test derisking and predictive uncertainty management in the design of damage-tolerant aerospace composite airframes.

entry.title: Variational Bayes for Variable Selection with Adaptive Sharing across Populations and Responses

link.title: Variational Bayes for Variable Selection with Adaptive Sharing across Populations and Responses

entry.content: We propose a variational Bayesian framework for variable selection with multiple responses across heterogeneous populations. The prior dependence among the inclusion indicators allows variable-selection information to be shared at different levels across populations and responses, while regression coefficients remain population- and response-specific. When the appropriate sharing structure is unknown, a data-driven rule adaptively determines the scope of information sharing from marginal association evidence. The resulting variational algorithm is computationally scalable and can be implemented using either individual-level or summary data. Under regularity conditions, we establish selection consistency and convergence properties of the variational parameters at fixed iterations of the algorithm for fixed dimension case. In high dimensions, we establish model-selection consistency and coefficient contraction in both $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ norms. Simulation studies show competitive variable selection performance and demonstrate the potential gains from joint analysis. We further illustrate the summary-data implementation using genome-wide association summary statistics from the 2021 Global Lipids Genetics Consortium study for four lipid traits across five populations.

entry.title: Generalized Posterior Calibration via Infinitesimal-Jackknife Variance Matching

link.title: Generalized Posterior Calibration via Infinitesimal-Jackknife Variance Matching

entry.content: Generalized posteriors update a prior through an exponential transformation of empirical loss rather than a conventional likelihood, with a learning rate controlling posterior concentration. Their credible intervals may have incorrect frequentist coverage because posterior dispersion need not reflect sampling variability. We propose infinitesimal-jackknife variance matching (IJVM), a computationally efficient method for selecting the learning rate for a prespecified scalar functional. IJVM matches the functional’s posterior variance to an infinitesimal-jackknife estimate of the sampling variance of its posterior mean, computed from posterior covariances with observation-level losses. A multiplicative one-step update requires one pilot posterior fit and a second fit for inference, avoiding explicit estimation of loss Hessians or gradient covariance matrices and repeated bootstrap posterior fitting. Under suitable regularity and Monte Carlo accuracy conditions, we establish consistency of the selected rate for the functional-specific first-order calibration target. With additional sampling and posterior-quantile assumptions, the resulting credible intervals achieve asymptotically nominal frequentist coverage. Simulations involving homoscedastic and heteroscedastic regression and hinge-loss classification show that one-step IJVM achieves coverage near the nominal 95% level, with interval lengths comparable to bootstrap-based generalized posterior calibration but substantially fewer posterior fits. Additional updates offer little improvement.

entry.title: Confidence Filtering in Video-Based Gait Assessment: Measurement Error versus Selection Shift

link.title: Confidence Filtering in Video-Based Gait Assessment: Measurement Error versus Selection Shift

entry.content: Video-based gait assessment often keeps only high-confidence pose observations, which can lower measurement error but change the movement assessed. We compared confidence selection with budget-matched random selection in a Parkinson-related cohort (n = 96) and an NF2-related replication cohort (n = 18). In the Parkinson-related cohort, confidence selection produced a small but consistent shift in the observed movement summary (+0.05 SD, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.07), while held-out Mini-BESTest error stayed flat (-0.04 points, -0.13 to 0.05); a policy preserving motion-group proportions reduced the shift, while NF2 showed no shift and its predictor did not beat a constant baseline. Because this shift mixes measurement error with selection shift, we decompose and simulate both on the cohort’s window structure. Filtering lowers local error when error depends on confidence, but biases the endpoint once confidence tracks movement more than error. In the Parkinson-related data, confidence was only weakly tied to movement (rho = 0.14). There, filtering is harmless if well-tracked windows are unbiased. If instead systematic error only redistributes within participants, filtering can add up to 0.58 degrees. Unchanged clinical error from such small-cohort predictors therefore cannot show that quality filtering preserves the assessed movement.

entry.title: Reference-based multiple imputation for longitudinal bounded discrete outcomes

link.title: Reference-based multiple imputation for longitudinal bounded discrete outcomes

entry.content: Reference-based multiple imputation has been developed for binary and ordinal responses. We develop a parsimonious formulation for longitudinal bounded scores and counts that preserves their finite integer support and gives partial and complete reference borrowing an explicit distributional interpretation. Discrete Kumaraswamy margins provide closed-form cumulative distribution and quantile functions, simplifying fitting and imputation under a Gaussian copula. Borrowing is defined through a regression model indexed by a smooth median anchor, allowing continuation under the assigned treatment, partial borrowing, or jump to reference after a specified trigger. With shapes shared across arms, complete borrowing replaces the active marginal distribution with the reference distribution at the same visit and covariate values, while conditional imputations remain informed by retained outcomes. Bayesian estimation uses latent variable augmentation, and all sensitivity rules share one fitted posterior. Completed datasets are analyzed using a beta-binomial random intercept model, with treatment comparisons expressed as standardized mean score differences. Simulations assess parameter recovery and imputation followed by analysis. An application to depression scores illustrates attenuation of the treatment benefit at the final visit as borrowing increases, with confidence intervals including zero under all rules.

entry.title: Outcome-dependent density combination by mixture Bayesian predictive synthesis

link.title: Outcome-dependent density combination by mixture Bayesian predictive synthesis

entry.content: In the problem of density combination, the decision maker receives multiple density functions and is tasked to learn which density is used most in which region of the outcome space, and to combine them into a single density. The outcome-dependent density combination can be cast as the Bayesian predictive synthesis, where the decision maker’s uncertainty is naturally integrated. The models for the outcome-dependent weights have been considered in Johnson and West (2025), but limited to the Gaussian density kernel. In this study, we point out the limitation of the model flexibility of the Gaussian weights, and theoretically and numerically verify that the estimated weights can be least outcome-dependent. As an alternative, we propose the use of the softmax (logistic-normal) functions as the models for the weights, together with the bias-adjustment to the submitted densities. The posterior computation is feasible by using the custom Metropolis-Hastings method with the P'olya-gamma augmentation. The utility of the proposed method is illustrated in the real data analysis of movie theatre revenues, where a human expert reports the point quantile forecasts without any uncertainty quantification.

The utility of the proposed method is illustrated in the real data analysis of movie theatre revenues, where a human expert reports the point quantile forecasts without any uncertainty quantification.

entry.title: Sequince: a modular sequential Monte Carlo toolkit

link.title: Sequince: a modular sequential Monte Carlo toolkit

entry.content: Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) methods approximate sequences of probability distributions using populations of weighted samples and are widely applicable, including in Bayesian inference and particle filtering. We present sequince, a modular Python toolkit for constructing SMC algorithms from reusable and extensible components. The toolkit provides modular steps for weighting, resampling, mutation, transformation, and control operations that are composed to implement different algorithms. It also includes prebuilt samplers for tempered SMC, persistent sampling and nested sampling via SMC. Its core components follow the Python Array API standard, supporting NumPy, JAX, PyTorch, and CuPy, enabling analyses on CPUs or GPUs. Random-number control and checkpointing support reproducible scientific workflows. This paper describes sequince v0.1.0 and its design as reusable infrastructure for methodological research and application of SMC methods.

entry.title: Adaptive Sequential Surveillance of Infectious Diseases Under Limited Sampling Capacity

link.title: Adaptive Sequential Surveillance of Infectious Diseases Under Limited Sampling Capacity

entry.content: This paper develops a closed-loop adaptive sequential surveillance framework for infectious disease monitoring with limited surveillance resources. In this framework, we use a Bayesian spatio-temporal model to predict disease prevalence at each location, and propose several adaptive site-allocation strategies based on the posterior probabilities that the predictions exceed a predefined threshold. These strategies exploit high-risk locations while also exploring, by random or recency-based sampling or by incorporating the frontiers of emerging outbreaks. To address the unequal inclusion probabilities induced by adaptive sampling, we integrate inverse-probability weighting (IPW) into each model update. A simulation study showed that adaptive surveillance strategies improved outbreak detection relative to uniform sampling and fixed sentinel sampling. Frontier-based strategies improved detection and timeliness relative to risk-proportional allocation. When IPW was used to update the model, some proposed strategies yielded lower inferential bias compared with the standard unweighted update, particularly for strategies that allowed more flexible exploration. Credible-interval coverage varied by strategy. The results identify trade-offs between exploitation of known high-risk locations and exploration of potential outbreak frontiers.

entry.title: Reinforcement Learning Under Runtime Confounding: Policy Learning and Off-Policy Evaluation

link.title: Reinforcement Learning Under Runtime Confounding: Policy Learning and Off-Policy Evaluation

entry.content: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used to train robust, adaptable systems across healthcare, e-commerce, and robotics. In these settings, legal, ethical, or logistical concerns may preclude certain key variables that drive decisions from being collected during deployment time. This gives rise to a setting known as runtime confounding: the logged data hold full observability, but deployment time lacks knowledge of certain variables, known as runtime confounders. Unlike single timepoint and non-adaptive settings, runtime confounding under reinforcement learning has the potential to propagate over time, as earlier decisions affect future states, observations, and action assignments, leading to biased learning. We address these problems with three contributions: we (1) develop policy learning algorithms under runtime-confounding, (2) develop semi-parametric efficient off-policy estimation procedures, and (3) provide diagnostics for understanding the price of runtime confounding.

entry.title: Graphical Modeling from Marginal Information via Optimal Transport

link.title: Graphical Modeling from Marginal Information via Optimal Transport

entry.content: A graphical model represents multivariate interactions through conditional independence, but requires jointly observed samples to be fitted to data. When individuals cannot be tracked and only marginal observations are available, as with destructive measurements leading to cross-sectional data, the problem of graphical modeling is confounded with that of assembling a joint law. We show how simultaneous graphical modeling and joint law assembly can be realized via a multi-marginal optimal transport problem with graphical cost. Focusing on Gaussian marginals, we generate a joint law satisfying the Markov properties prescribed by a given graph. Within the class of joint distributions respecting the graph and marginals constraints, our construction selects a member by making the interactions set by the graph as strong as possible under a dependence budget measured by relative entropy. In the empirical setting, where only estimates of the marginals are available, we examine the stability of the problem under perturbations of both the marginals and of the graph weights. The resulting error splits into an estimation term, vanishing with the sample size, and a specification term, which quantifies the cost of a misspecified graph. Finally, we illustrate these findings by numerical experiments.

entry.title: Graphical Models Induced by Irreversible Event Accumulation on Trees

link.title: Graphical Models Induced by Irreversible Event Accumulation on Trees

entry.content: Decomposable graphical models are usually adopted for their computational convenience rather than derived from a data-generating mechanism. We show that a special class of them arises naturally from the irreversible accumulation of events along a branching history. Each event is attached to an edge of a latent rooted tree and is inherited by everything below that edge; an observation records which events have occurred at a randomly chosen node, not necessarily a leaf. When the tree is a path, this is the cumulative coding of an ordinal variable, whose indicators form a Markov chain; in the general tree case the Markov chain is replaced by a junction tree. The conditional independence graph of the event indicators is always decomposable and, in fact, is the line graph of the tree (maximal cliques correspond to nodes where two or more edges meet and separators are the single events on the edges joining two such nodes). The graph determines the tree up to the choice of root. A connected graph arises in this way if, and only if, it is chordal, any two of its maximal cliques share at most one vertex, no vertex is in three maximal cliques, and the graph is such that any two maximal cliques share at most one vertex. This provides a simple graphical test for compatibility with the mechanism (necessary but not sufficient, as irreversibility also constrains the distribution’s support). The structure breaks down if we look at just the leaves, and measurement error destroys the exact screening and leads to a denser graph rather than simply a weaker dependence. We discuss inference, provide diagnostics for departures such as recurrent events, illustrate them on some simulated data and discuss their application in the context of mutation accumulation and lineage tracing where both ancestral and descendant types are sampled together.

entry.title: Beyond $\chi^2$: Ensemble null tests for reliable scientific discovery

link.title: Beyond $\chi^2$: Ensemble null tests for reliable scientific discovery

entry.content: Unrecognized systematic errors can survive standard checks and undermine scientific discoveries. Null tests and experimental controls can expose these failures, but averaging measurements or reducing them to scalar statistics can hide important structure. We propose ensemble null tests that compare multivariate distributions with references from observations or simulations. We demonstrate their benefits across science. In cosmic microwave background simulations, they detect systematic effects missed by conventional $\chi^2$ tests. In Gaia data, they detect velocity asymmetry as sensitively as an informed search. In a CRISPR screen, they expose a control mismatch in DNA damage and reveal which cellular profiles drive it. As scientific datasets grow, ensemble testing turns repeated measurements into a broader search for unknown unknowns, strengthening the empirical foundation for scientific discovery.

entry.title: Homogeneity Pursuit of Panel Data with Sparsity

link.title: Homogeneity Pursuit of Panel Data with Sparsity

entry.content: In panel data analysis, studying individual attributes is important for both methodological development and practical applications. Homogeneity in individual attributes and sparsity in coefficients are therefore important topics, as they help uncover relationships among individuals and identify the truly relevant covariates. However, many existing approaches do not explicitly exploit the potential grouping information contained in separately fitted individual-level penalized estimators to identify latent groups. To address this gap, we propose a hierarchical group recovery approach based on sparse initial estimation to jointly identify latent groups and sparse parameter structures in panel data. We first introduce a basic version that can efficiently identify homogeneity and sparsity. Based on this basic version, we further introduce a local search step to improve the performance of our method. Compared with existing methods, our approach shows the best overall performance when jointly considering estimation accuracy and computational efficiency. The simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness and advantages of our approach over existing approaches. We further apply the proposed approach to a real dataset to show its practical applicability.
